objectives: Explain erosion, longshore drift and the formation of coastal landforms
Evaluate hard and soft coastal management, including mangroves

blocks.title: Waves and erosion
blocks.md: **Constructive waves** are low and long, with a strong swash and weak backwash: they build beaches. **Destructive waves** are high and steep, with a weak swash and strong backwash: they remove material. Erosion processes: **hydraulic action**, **abrasion**, **attrition**, **solution**. Weathering and mass movement also shape cliffs.

blocks.title: Landforms
blocks.md: **Erosion:** cliffs with a wave-cut notch and platform; headlands, caves, arches and stacks. **Deposition:** beaches, spits (a ridge of sand or shingle attached to land at one end), bars and tombolos, formed where **longshore drift** carries material along the coast, driven by waves arriving at an angle. Rivers deliver sediment to deltas, estuaries and mangrove coasts.

items.text: Net movement of sand and shingle

blocks.caption: Longshore drift moves sand in a zigzag along the beach.
blocks.alt: Zigzag arrows: swash runs up at an angle and backwash returns straight, moving sand along the beach.

blocks.title: Management
blocks.md: **Hard engineering:** sea walls, groynes, rip-rap: effective locally but costly and can starve other beaches. **Soft engineering:** beach nourishment, dune restoration, mangrove protection and replanting. **Managed retreat** lets the sea reclaim land. Mangroves line parts of the Cameroonian coast and estuaries; they protect shores, shelter fish nurseries and supply wood, but they are cut for fuel and building.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.md:
- Swash is the wave running up the beach; backwash is the return flow.
- Longshore drift is a movement along the coast, not onto it.
- Hard engineering protects one place but may increase erosion downdrift.
- Do not describe a stack as a cave: the order is cave, arch, stack, stump.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Spit formation
blocks.statement: Explain briefly how a spit forms.
steps: Waves arriving at an angle move sand along the beach by longshore drift.
Where the coastline changes direction, for example at a river mouth, the material continues in a straight line into deeper water.
Deposition builds a ridge attached to land at one end.
Wave refraction and wind may curve the end.
blocks.answer: Longshore drift deposits material where the coast bends, building a ridge attached at one end.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Management choice
blocks.statement: A fishing village on a sandy coast is losing land. Suggest and justify one management approach.
steps: Option: protect or restore mangroves and dunes, with groynes only if needed.
Mangroves absorb wave energy, trap sediment and support fisheries, at low cost.
A concrete wall would be costly and could shift erosion to neighbouring beaches.
blocks.answer: Soft approach: restore mangroves/dunes for cheap, sustainable protection.

blocks.title: Glaciers
blocks.md: A **glacier** is a large body of ice that moves slowly under gravity. It forms where more snow falls than melts: snow is compressed into **firn** and then ice. During the ice ages of the Pleistocene, ice sheets covered large parts of the northern hemisphere; the last glacial maximum was roughly 20 000 years ago.

blocks.title: Erosion and landforms
blocks.md: Glaciers erode by **plucking** (tearing blocks from rock) and **abrasion** (scraping by rock debris). Landforms: **corries** (armchair hollows), **arêtes** (sharp ridges between corries), **pyramidal peaks**, **U-shaped valleys**, **hanging valleys** and **ribbon lakes**.

items.text: Compaction forms firn then glacial ice
Plucking and abrasion erode the valley

blocks.caption: From snow to a valley glacier that erodes.
blocks.alt: Four boxes connected by arrows: snow, firn and ice, ice flow, erosion by plucking and abrasion.

blocks.title: Deposition
blocks.md: Melting ice drops **till**, forming **moraines** (lateral, medial, terminal), **drumlins** and scattered **erratics** (rocks from far away). Meltwater forms outwash plains and eskers.

blocks.title: Glaciers in Africa
blocks.md: Tropical Africa has no large ice sheets. A few small glaciers exist on the highest mountains of East Africa and have been shrinking; they are not found in Cameroon. Questions on glaciation usually use northern European, Alpine or Himalayan examples.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Form of a U-shaped valley
blocks.statement: Explain how a U-shaped valley forms.
steps: A river valley is V-shaped before glaciation.
Ice fills the valley and erodes the floor and sides by plucking and abrasion.
The valley becomes wider and deeper, with steep sides and a flat floor.
After the ice melts the typical U-shaped cross-section remains.
blocks.answer: Glacial plucking and abrasion widen and deepen a V-valley into a U.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Corries and arêtes
steps: Two corries develop on opposite sides of a mountain.
Erosion by plucking and abrasion cuts back the back walls.
The land between them is narrowed to a steep, knife-edge ridge: the arête.
blocks.answer: Back-to-back corries leave a narrow ridge.

blocks.title: Stores and flows
blocks.md: **Stores:** oceans, atmosphere, ice, groundwater, rivers, soil moisture, vegetation. **Flows:** evaporation, **transpiration**, condensation, precipitation, **interception**, **infiltration**, percolation, **throughflow**, surface run-off, groundwater flow. A **drainage basin** is the area drained by a river and its tributaries, bounded by a watershed.

blocks.title: Water balance
blocks.md: $P = Q + E \pm \Delta S$, where P is precipitation, Q is run-off (streamflow), E is evapotranspiration and ΔS is the change in storage. If the soil is not storing or losing water, $Q = P - E$.

items.text: Rivers and groundwater return to the sea

blocks.caption: The hydrological cycle.
blocks.alt: Five boxes with arrows from evaporation to condensation, precipitation, ground processes and the return to the sea.

blocks.title: Water resources
blocks.md: Groundwater held in **aquifers** reaches the surface through wells and springs; the top of the saturated zone is the **water table**. In Africa, rainfall is seasonal and unreliable in many places. Dams (such as Lagdo on the Benue) store water for power and irrigation; boreholes and rainwater harvesting provide drinking water; poor sanitation spreads water-borne disease.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Infiltration is water entering the soil; percolation is deeper movement; throughflow is sideways flow in the soil.
- Transpiration is water loss by plants; evaporation from surfaces; together evapotranspiration.
- Dams bring benefits but also costs: displacement of people, silting and changes downstream.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Water balance
blocks.statement: A basin receives 1500 mm of rain a year and loses 700 mm by evapotranspiration. Assuming no change in storage, find run-off.

blocks.title: Example 2 — With storage
blocks.statement: In a dry year P = 900 mm, E = 700 mm and the soil and groundwater store 50 mm less water at the end of the year (ΔS = −50). Find Q.
steps: Q = 200 + 50 = 250 mm: stored water has fed the river.

exercises.prompt: Explain why a sea wall can reduce erosion at one place but cause problems elsewhere.
exercises.model: A sea wall reflects wave energy and stops cliffs or land retreating where it stands. But it prevents the supply of sediment from the cliff and may bounce waves downward, scouring the beach in front. Down-drift areas lose sand and erode faster.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Describe the formation of caves, arches and stacks and evaluate two methods of managing a retreating coastline.
exercises.model: Waves attack cracks in a headland by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a cave. The cave erodes through the headland to form an arch. The roof collapses leaving a stack, which later becomes a stump. Management: sea walls give strong local protection but are expensive; mangrove and dune restoration is cheaper and sustainable but slower and less certain against severe storms.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: With the help of diagrams, describe how a glacier changes a river valley and what features remain after the ice has melted.
exercises.model: Before glaciation the river valley is V-shaped with interlocking spurs. A glacier fills it, straightening and deepening it by abrasion and plucking, truncating spurs and widening the sides into a U-shape. Tributary valleys are left hanging, with waterfalls. Ribbon lakes fill over-deepened parts, and moraines mark ice limits.
